properties.entry: A component that is private for now
A realistic application built only from these widgets: 2,500 contacts searched by facets with live counts, find bars, a split panel and a JSON grid you can sort, page, rearrange and export as CSV.

A data grid whose rows are rendered in the browser from JSON and per-column HTML templates instead of Wicket components: one light component that sorts, pages, edits in a modal and repaints rows pushed live over a websocket. The same grid in React and Svelte.
The same grid built the classic Wicket way: every row made of Wicket components and columns on the server and repainted via Ajax, looking and behaving exactly like the JSON grid.

An infinite list of a thousand cards: the server sends the users as JSON, 24 at a time as you scroll, and the browser renders each card from an HTML template; clicks on a card reach the server as actions.

The tree of life twice: as a tree of Wicket components expanded via Ajax, and as one component rendered in the browser from JSON, loading its branches on demand and driven fully by the keyboard (WAI-ARIA).

A tree with columns: the scientific names, ranks and periods of the tree of life, as a Wicket table tree or rendered in the browser from JSON as a WAI-ARIA tree grid, with lazily loaded branches and resizable columns.
Two grids working together: choose a country in the master, rendered in the browser from JSON, and the detail, rendered on the server by Wicket components, shows its users via Ajax.
Known and unknown progress driven by an Ajax timer, on the native progress element with moving stripes, so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
Toasts in any corner of the window, of four types or the page's own, closed by the user or after a countdown; in Wicket the page's feedback messages become notifications by themselves.

A drop-down in the colors of the theme that replaces the native select: one or many values as chips, opened, filtered and navigated by keyboard in the browser, while forms and Ajax work as with a plain select.
Suggestions fetched via Ajax as JSON and rendered in the browser from templates, flags and all: one or many values as chips, or a find bar handing each pick to the page.
Choosing several values out of many, even thousands: two lists with a filter, drag and drop, keyboard moves and their own order, drawn lazily in the browser and posted like a plain select.

Date and time pickers that speak every locale: the format of the field, the language of the calendar, the first day of the week and the 12- or 24-hour clock; typed or picked, by mouse or keyboard, checked on the server.
One look for the buttons of Wicket, React and Svelte: four variants, three sizes, a text, an icon or both, actions via Ajax, and any link or form button turned into one by a behavior.
Slim scroll bars in the colors of the theme that look the same in every browser, drawn over native scrolling so the wheel, the keys and touch work as ever, and following content changed via Ajax.
Panes that share the space, nested as in an IDE: drag the divider or move it with the keyboard, collapse a pane, size in percent or pixels, and let the server know and remember the layout.
A desktop inside the page: floating windows that are not modal, with a taskbar; they move, fold, resize, minimize, maximize, tile and cascade, each holding real components such as the grids.

Add, edit and delete in a modal dialog that keeps the focus, drags and folds by its title and asks before discarding changes; the same dialog in Wicket, React and Svelte over one shared REST resource.

Make a theme of your own: pick its colors and watch grids, tabs, dialogs and notifications follow live, then copy the CSS class that defines it. No inline style, so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
